Question: How can God be three and one at the same time?
ShortAnswer: God is three and one because 'one' describes what God is (one divine essence) and 'three' describes who God is (three persons). It is a mystery, not a contradiction: God is not one person and three persons, but one God in three persons.
DetailedAnswer: The apparent contradiction dissolves when you see that 'one' and 'three' answer different questions. God is one in essence — one divine nature, one will, one power. And God is three in person — Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, each fully God, each distinct from the others, relating to one another in love. Jesus said, 'I and the Father are one' (John 10:30) — one in essence — yet He prayed to the Father (John 17), showing distinction of persons. The Spirit is sent by the Father and the Son (John 14:16-17, 26), yet is fully God. Common analogies all break down: water as ice, liquid, and steam suggests one person changing forms (the ancient error of modalism); an egg's shell, white, and yolk suggests parts of God (but each person is fully God, not a third of Him); a shamrock has three leaves but they are not persons. Analogies fail because nothing in creation is exactly like God — and that is the point. The Trinity is not a math puzzle to solve but a mystery to worship: a God who is, in Himself, a communion of love — which is why love is not something God merely does, but something He eternally is (1 John 4:8).
